text:
maya: Heads-up — saw CA repeatedly choose small-cpu nodegroups instead of spinning up GPU nodegroups during the ML batch burst at 04:12 UTC. Result: ~6 jobs pending with pod affinity/gpu requests, lots of pending '0/...' and then timeouts.

leo: Ugh. Are GPU groups marked with a lower priority by CA? We recently set expander=least-waste to reduce cost.

maya: Yep, that might be the culprit — least-waste prefers filling existing nodes before creating a big expensive GPU. For GPU workloads that require dedicated nodes, least-waste can be counterproductive.

nora: Options: switch expander to a priority-based strategy or tweak scale-up heuristics to prefer nodegroups with gpus when pods request nvidia.com/gpu. Also can annotate nodegroups with autoscaler-priority.

sam: I can prototype a canary: set expander=priority and add priorities for nodegroups. Also lower --new-pod-scale-up-delay so CA reacts faster to pods that specifically request GPUs.

maya: Nice. Let's capture the rough helm/values snippet I planned for the canary.

leo: paste it here pls.

sam: ```yaml
controller:
  extraArgs:
    expander: "priority"
    --scale-down-unneeded-time: "10m"
    --scale-down-utilization-threshold: "0.36"
    --max-node-provision-time: "15m"
    --max-empty-bulk-delete: "2"
    --new-pod-scale-up-delay: "5s"
    --skip-nodes-with-local-storage: "false"

# priority map via arg or configmap, example:
# priority: ng-gpu=100,ng-gpu-preemptible=80,ng-cpu=10
```

nora: For nodegroup labels you can do: `kubectl label nodegroup/ng-gpu autoscaler-priority=100` (or set it on the cloud node pool / ASG tag). CA priority expander reads those tags/labels.

maya: ops question: risk of overprovisioning costly GPUs? If priority forces GPU pools open, we might spend more.

sam: We mitigate with 1) lower scale-up aggression (keep max-node-provision-time sensible), 2) short scale-down-unneeded-time so idle GPUs come down if not used, 3) max-empty-bulk-delete to avoid mass empty deletes interfering with scale-up. Also add a budget alert for GPU-hour spend.

leo: Another idea: gate GPU expander preference on pod label selector (only prefer GPUs when pods have label "workload-type: gpu-batch") — prevents realtime services from forcing GPUs. That requires small webhook or CA upstream support.

nora: There's also the approach of taints+tolerations: keep GPU nodegroups tainted and only allow pods that tolerate to land. CA will still scale them if pod pending with toleration+gpu request. That reduces accidental scheduling.

autoscaler-bot: [04:29 UTC] scale event: group ng-cpu scaled +3 -> 12 (reason: urgent pending pods).

maya: Thanks. Proposed rollout plan:
1) Canary in staging cluster: change expander to priority + annotate nodegroups (ng-gpu=100, ng-cpu=10).
2) Tune flags as in snippet, especially --new-pod-scale-up-delay=5s and --scale-down-unneeded-time=10m.
3) Add monitoring: pending pods broken down by resource request, GPU-hour burn alert, and CA scale decisions logging.
4) After 24h validate pending GPU pods metric and cost delta, then roll to prod.

sam: I'll open a PR with helm values and an ops-runbook for rollback. Tagging @nora for monitoring dashboards.

nora: On it — will add a cheap QPS metric and a dashboard panel showing "pending gpu pods" + CA decision logs.

leo: One small tweak: we should also set `--max-node-provision-time` to 20m in prod (because GPUs sometimes take longer to boot) so CA doesn't give up prematurely. Keep canary at 15m.

maya: Agree. I'll create the canary ticket and mark it P2. If we see regressions we revert expander and revert flags back.

sam: PR link when ready.

autoscaler-bot: [04:41 UTC] alert: pending_gpu_pods > 3 for 7m, notify #oncall.

maya: Thanks everyone — follow-ups in the PR thread.

(attachments: logs + pod snippets referenced, linked in the PR)
